parts.prompt: Explain why CO can be absent from the predicted rate law even though it is consumed overall.

steps.text: Overall: NO₂+CO→NO+CO₂.
NO₃ is an intermediate: formed in one step and consumed in the next, absent from the overall equation.
v=k[NO₂]² under the stated slow-first-step model.
The slow elementary step is bimolecular.
CO participates only in the subsequent fast step in this proposed mechanism; it is not involved in the rate-determining elementary event.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate both forward step activation energies and identify the larger barrier.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the overall reaction enthalpy and distinguish an intermediate from a transition state.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the absolute heights of the peaks alone are insufficient for comparing the step barriers.

steps.text: Step 1: 45−0=45 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: 50−(−20)=70 kJ mol⁻¹; the second barrier is larger.
ΔH=−60 kJ mol⁻¹.
An intermediate occupies a local energy minimum and has a finite lifetime; a transition state is an energy maximum along the reaction path.
Each activation energy must be measured from the energy of the species immediately preceding that transition state.

title: A fair rate comparison
stem: A student compares reaction rates using 1.0 g powdered CaCO₃ with 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl, and 2.0 g chips with 50 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl. The student concludes that particle size alone caused the difference.

verification.method: Author derivation and automated schema, rendering and numerical checks

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify two confounding variables and describe a fairer comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State a suitable rate measurement and explain why repeats are useful.

steps.text: The mass of CaCO₃ and the acid concentration differ; accept acid volume as another confounder.
Use equal masses of the same solid and identical acid volume, concentration and starting temperature, changing only particle size.
Measure initial CO₂ volume produced per unit time, or initial mass loss per unit time.
Repeats show random variation and allow a mean and spread to be estimated; they do not automatically remove systematic bias.

steps.text: $K_c=[\mathrm{HI}]^2/([\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{I_2}])$.
Products are favoured in the equilibrium expression at this temperature.
K does not determine how rapidly equilibrium is reached or imply complete conversion.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why applying “higher pressure favours fewer gas molecules” without considering how pressure is changed is misleading here.

steps.text: Total pressure increases.
The equilibrium amounts of N₂O₄ and NO₂ do not change under the ideal-gas assumption.
The partial pressures/concentrations of the reacting gases are unchanged at fixed volume.
Only the inert-gas contribution to total pressure increases, so the reacting system is not driven away from equilibrium.

steps.text: Qc>Kc, so the reverse direction is favoured, consuming PCl₃ and Cl₂.

steps.text: Use ΔG°=−RT ln K with dimensionless K.
At 300 K: −3.46 kJ mol⁻¹; at 350 K: −1.18 kJ mol⁻¹.
The forward reaction is exothermic.
Heating lowers K and favours reactants, so heat is a product of the forward process.
Equilibrium constants express thermodynamic composition; the rate depends on activation barriers and kinetic conditions.
